# irender-map-kit

Maps for [iRender](https://github.com/kaushik-xs/iRender/blob/main/README.md) documents, on OpenStreetMap or Google Maps. Markers, popups, clusters, shapes and buttons are the kit's own, in the theme's colours, so a document looks and works the same on both.

```rust
let mut engine = irender_html::Engine::new();
irender_map_kit::register(&mut engine.registry);
```

From the CLI, add `--map-kit` to `validate`, `render` or `components`:

```sh
cargo run -p irender-cli -- render examples/maps/gallery.yaml --data examples/maps/gallery.data.json \
  --ui-kit --map-kit -o maps.html
```

[`examples/maps/gallery.yaml`](https://github.com/kaushik-xs/iRender/blob/main/examples/maps/gallery.yaml) shows each feature, and [`examples/blocks/map-01.yaml`](https://github.com/kaushik-xs/iRender/blob/main/examples/blocks/map-01.yaml) is a page with a list beside a map.

## A map

```yaml
- type: ui-map
  props:
    markers:
      - { id: hq, lat: 12.9716, lng: 77.5946, title: Head office, description: Open until 6 pm }
      - { id: lab, lat: 12.9352, lng: 77.6245, title: Lab, tone: info }
```

The view fits what's on the map, unless there's a `center` (`[lat, lng]` or `{ lat, lng }`) and `zoom`. Both can come from state, and the map moves when they change.

## OpenStreetMap or Google Maps

| `provider` | drawn by | key | library |
|---|---|---|---|
| `osm` (default) | [Leaflet](https://leafletjs.com/) 1.9.4 and OpenStreetMap's tiles | none | about 43 KB gzipped, from jsDelivr |
| `google` | Google Maps' JavaScript API | needed | from Google |

Neither is inlined: a page loads the one it uses, once, when a map comes near the view. If the host page has `window.L` or `google.maps` already, the kit uses that.

```rust
use irender_map_kit::{MapKit, Tiles};

irender_map_kit::register_with(&mut engine.registry, MapKit {
    leaflet: "/static/leaflet/".into(),          // your own copy of leaflet.js and leaflet.css
    tiles: Tiles { url: "https://tiles.example.com/{z}/{x}/{y}.png".into(), ..Tiles::default() },
    google_key: Some("…".into()),
});
```

- **OpenStreetMap's tiles** are run by volunteers for light use: see their [tile usage policy](https://operations.osmfoundation.org/policies/tiles/). For a busy site, set `tiles` (on the kit or on a map) to your own tile server or a provider's. They need to know which site asks, so serve pages over HTTP; one opened as a file may be refused.
- **Attribution** shows in the corner, and the map data's licence asks for it. Set `attribution` and `attributionUrl` with your own `tiles`.
- **Google's key** comes from `google_key`, the CLI's `--google-maps-key`, the `GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY` environment variable or a map's `apiKey`. Browsers see it, so restrict it to your sites in Google's console. `mapId` and `mapType` are Google's own.
- **Dark mode:** Google's maps switch to its dark colours. OpenStreetMap's tiles are darkened with a filter (`darkTiles: false` leaves them), or `tiles.darkUrl` gives dark ones.

## Markers

Rows with a place: `lat` and `lng` (or `latitude`, `lon`, `long`, `longitude`, or `position: [lat, lng]`). Rows without one are left out.

| field | |
|---|---|
| `id` | Names it in state (default: its index) |
| `title`, `description`, `href` | The popup; `title` (or `name`) also names it for screen readers |
| `label` | Up to three characters in the pin: a letter, a number, an emoji |
| `tone`, `color` | `neutral`, `info`, `success`, `warning`, `danger`, `primary`; or any CSS colour |
| `alarm`, `effect` | In alarm; or `pulse`, `glow`, `bounce` or `blink` (see [Alarms](#alarms)) |
| `draggable` | This one can, or can't, be dragged |

- **Other field names:** `latField`, `lngField` and `titleField`.
- **Colour by a field:** `toneBy: { field: status, tones: { late: danger, done: success } }`.
- **Filtering:** `filter` takes the same conditions as `ui-data-table` and `ui-chart`, so one `ui-filters` panel can narrow a map, a table and a chart.
- **Clusters:** `cluster: true` groups markers closer than 56px (or give the px) until there's room for them. Clicking a group zooms to it.
- **Many:** past 300 markers, only those near the view are in the page.

## Alarms

```yaml
- type: ui-map
  props:
    markers: "{{ machines }}"
    alarmBy: { field: status, values: [ fault, offline ] }
    effectBy: { field: status, effects: { overdue: glow } }
    bindAlarms: alarms
```

A marker in alarm (`alarmBy`, or `alarm: true` on its row) pulses in red with a `!` on it, unless the row has its own tone, effect or label. It stays above the rest, a group with one in it turns red and pulses too, and `bindAlarms` has the ids. When one starts, screen readers hear it and the map fires `alarm` (`{ id, marker }`), which `on` can act on, e.g. to open a toast.

`effect` animates any marker: `pulse` (rings going out from the place), `glow` (a halo that breathes), `bounce`, or `blink` (slowly, once a second). With reduced motion asked for, they hold still: `pulse` and `glow` keep a ring and a halo, and `bounce` and `blink` show nothing.

## State

| prop | the state key |
|---|---|
| `bind` | the selected marker's id; setting it selects that marker and brings it into view |
| `bindMarker` | the selected marker itself, or null |
| `bindVisible` | the ids of the markers in view, e.g. for a list beside the map |
| `bindView` | `{ center, zoom, bounds: { north, south, east, west } }` |
| `bindAlarms` | the ids of the markers in alarm |
| `bindPoint` | `{ lat, lng }`: clicking the map puts a pin there, which can be dragged |
| `bindMarkers` | the rows, with a dragged marker's new place (with `draggable`) |
| `bindShape` | the id of the shape last clicked |
| `bindLocation` | `{ lat, lng, accuracy }`, after My location |

## Popups and panels

The selected marker opens a popup with its title, description and link (`popup: false` for none). A `ui-map-popup` is the popup's content instead, with the marker in scope as `marker`. A `ui-map-panel` floats above the map.

```yaml
- type: ui-map
  props: { markers: "{{ jobs }}", bind: job }
  children:
    - type: ui-map-popup
      children:
        - { type: text, props: { value: "{{ marker.customer }}" } }
        - { type: ui-progress, props: { value: "{{ marker.progress }}" } }
    - type: ui-map-panel
      props: { position: top-right }
      children: [ { type: ui-badge, props: { text: Live, dot: true } } ]
```

## Shapes

```yaml
shapes:
  - { id: zone, type: circle, center: [40.4168, -3.7038], radius: "{{ radius }}", tone: primary, title: Delivery zone }
  - { id: way, type: line, points: [[40.41, -3.70], [40.42, -3.69]], tone: info, width: 4, dashed: true }
  - { id: park, type: area, points: [[40.415, -3.69], [40.42, -3.68], [40.41, -3.68]], tone: success, fill: 0.3 }
```

`radius` is in metres. An area's `points` can be a list of rings, the first its outline and the rest holes. `geojson` takes a GeoJSON object: lines and areas take their look from `properties`, and points become markers. A shape with a `title`, or any with `bindShape`, can be clicked.

## Overlays

```yaml
overlays:
  - { id: plan, type: image, url: floor-plan.svg, bounds: [[52.45, 13.3], [52.4515, 13.304]], opacity: "{{ strength }}" }
  - { id: marks, type: tiles, url: "https://tiles.openseamap.org/seamark/{z}/{x}/{y}.png", attribution: © OpenSeaMap contributors }
  - { id: busy, type: heat, points: "{{ sites }}", weightField: people, radius: 40, show: "{{ busy }}" }
```

They lie over the map and under its shapes and markers. Each has `opacity` (0 to 1) and `show`, so a switch or a slider can drive it.

- **`image`:** a picture stretched over its `bounds` (`[[south, west], [north, east]]`, or `{ north, south, east, west }`): a floor plan, an old map, a drone photo. It can't be turned. The view fits it.
- **`tiles`:** another tile server's, usually see-through: sea marks, rainfall, railways. Give its `attribution`, and `maxZoom` if it has none closer.
- **`heat`:** where rows are, by how many, or by `weightField`. `radius` is in px on the screen and `max` is the weight that counts in full (default: the greatest). Also takes `[lat, lng, weight]`.

## Commands and events

Send a command with the `call` action. `map` names the map by its element id; a page with one map doesn't need it.

| `call` | |
|---|---|
| `map.select` | Selects `args.id`, or nothing when it's null |
| `map.center` | Moves to `args.id`, or to `args.lat` and `args.lng`, at `args.zoom` |
| `map.fit` | Fits everything, or `args.ids` |
| `map.zoomin`, `map.zoomout`, `map.locate` | As the buttons |

`on` hears `markerselect` (`{ id, marker }`), `markermove` (`{ id, lat, lng }`), `alarm` (`{ id, marker }`), `shapeselect` (`{ id, shape }`), `mapclick` (`{ lat, lng }`), `viewchange` and `locate`.

## Gestures and keys

`gestures: cooperative` (the default) lets the page scroll past a map: Ctrl / ⌘ + wheel or two fingers zoom it. On OpenStreetMap, one finger on a touch screen scrolls the page, and the buttons, keys and two fingers move the map. `greedy` gives the map the wheel and one finger, for a map that fills the page, and `none` keeps it still.

| key | |
|---|---|
| Tab | The markers and groups in turn |
| Enter | Opens a marker's popup and moves into it |
| Escape | Closes the popup, back to its marker |
| Alt + arrows | Moves a draggable marker |
| Arrows, `+`, `-` | Pan and zoom, with the map focused |

## Safety

Marker and shape text is shown as text. A marker's `href` can't run a script, and with `Engine::untrusted()` it has to be a web, mail or phone link. Tile and overlay URLs in a document pass its policy. The key and Leaflet's address come from the host unless the document sets `apiKey`.

## When it can't load

The map says so, and lists the places.

## Not built yet

See [PENDING.md](https://github.com/kaushik-xs/iRender/blob/main/PENDING.md#map-kit-next-phases).


---


# irender-twin-kit

Digital twins for [iRender](https://github.com/kaushik-xs/iRender/blob/main/README.md) documents: 3D worlds drawn with [three.js](https://threejs.org/) from models of most formats, with machine and sensor data on them. Everything in a world is configuration, and any of it may use state: the models, where things stand, the paths they drive, zones, walls, the ground, the light and the camera's views. Tags, popups and buttons are the kit's own elements, in the theme's colours.

```rust
let mut engine = irender_html::Engine::new();
irender_twin_kit::register(&mut engine.registry);
```

From the CLI, add `--twin-kit` to `validate`, `render` or `components`:

```sh
cargo run -p irender-cli -- render examples/twin/world.yaml --ui-kit --twin-kit -o twin/world.html
```

[`examples/twin/`](https://github.com/kaushik-xs/iRender/blob/main/examples/twin) has a page per feature, linked from its [index](https://github.com/kaushik-xs/iRender/blob/main/examples/twin/index.yaml). The blocks are whole pages: [`twin-01`](https://github.com/kaushik-xs/iRender/blob/main/examples/blocks/twin-01.yaml) a packing hall with live machine data, [`twin-02`](https://github.com/kaushik-xs/iRender/blob/main/examples/blocks/twin-02.yaml) a cold store's temperature sensors, [`twin-03`](https://github.com/kaushik-xs/iRender/blob/main/examples/blocks/twin-03.yaml) a layout planner, and [`twin-04`](https://github.com/kaushik-xs/iRender/blob/main/examples/blocks/twin-04.yaml) a dairy's bottling line with its food safety checks. Their models are NVIDIA SimReady assets ([credits](https://github.com/kaushik-xs/iRender/blob/main/examples/twin/models/CREDITS.md)).

## A world

```yaml
- type: ui-twin
  props:
    height: 480
    models:
      rack: models/rack.glb
      forklift: models/forklift.glb
    objects:
      - { id: r1, model: rack, position: [-4, -3], title: Rack 1 }
      - { id: f1, model: forklift, path: aisle, speed: 1.2, title: Forklift }
      - { id: pillar, shape: box, size: [0.4, 3, 0.4], position: [0, 3] }
    paths:
      - { id: aisle, points: [[-2, -5], [-2, 4], [6, 4], [6, -5]], closed: true, flow: true }
    zones:
      - { id: store, center: [-4, -1.5], size: [6, 6], tone: info, label: Storage }
    walls:
      - { points: [[-8, -6], [8, -6], [8, 6], [-8, 6]], closed: true, height: 1.2, opacity: 0.5 }
    views:
      - { id: overview, label: Overview, position: [9, 11, 13], target: [0, 0, 0] }
```

Units are metres, with y up. A `position` is `[x, z]` on the ground or `[x, y, z]`. A `rotation` is degrees about the vertical, or `[x, y, z]`.

| prop | what it is |
|---|---|
| `models` | The models by name: a URL, or `{ url, units, up, scale, fit, rotate, origin, format, mtl, color }` |
| `objects` | What's in the world, as rows: `{ id, model or shape, position, rotation, scale, title, … }`. Every other field is the object's data |
| `paths` | Routes that objects follow, drawn on the ground, with `flow` stripes moving along them |
| `zones` | Areas on the ground (`points`, or `center` and `size`), with a `label`, a `tone`, and a `height` for a volume |
| `walls` | Walls along `points`, with a `height`, `thickness` and `opacity` |
| `ground` | `{ size, center, color, grid }`, or `false`. By default it's big enough for everything, with a 1 m grid |
| `environment` | `{ preset: studio, day or night, light, shadows, background, fog }` |
| `camera` | `{ position, target, fov }`; the camera moves there when it changes. By default it fits the world |
| `views` | Named camera places, shown as buttons; `bindView` keeps the current one in state |
| `world` | All of these in one object, e.g. a layout kept in state. A prop of its own wins |
| `src` | The URL of such a world as JSON, fetched in the browser |

`shape` draws an object without a model: `box` (`size: [w, h, d]`), `cylinder` and `cone` (`[diameter, height]`), `sphere`, `sensor` (a small sphere coloured by its value), or `point` (nothing, only its tag).

## Models

Any model three.js can open works, picked by the file's extension, a `data:` address's type (`data:model/gltf-binary;base64,…`) or `format`:

| format | notes |
|---|---|
| glTF, GLB | Best for the web. Draco and meshopt meshes, and KTX2 textures, are read. Animations play with `animation: true` or a clip's name on the object |
| OBJ | With its materials when `mtl` names the `.mtl` file |
| FBX, DAE (Collada), 3MF, 3DS, WRL (VRML) | |
| STL, PLY | Meshes without materials; `color` gives one |
| USD, USDA, USDC, USDZ | three.js's own reader. A USD that refers to other files, as NVIDIA's SimReady assets do, is better converted to GLB first (below) |

Models come in many units and orientations. Each is put right once, when it's loaded:

- `units`: `m` (the default), `cm`, `mm`, `in` or `ft`.
- `up: z` for models with z up (CAD, USD).
- `scale`, `rotate` (degrees), or `fit`: the largest side in metres, or `[w, h, d]` to fit inside.
- `origin`: `base` (the default) stands it on the ground at its middle; `center` or `none` keep more of it as it was.

A model is loaded once however many objects use it, and each object shares its meshes and materials until something (`opacity`, an animation, an effect that glows or blinks) needs its own. One that fails to load is drawn as a wireframe box, and the twin fires `failed` with the model's name.

### Simpler far away

Far from the camera, a model can be drawn with fewer triangles: from some metres off nobody sees a drum's rivets, and a hall of a thousand detailed machines is tens of millions of triangles otherwise.

```yaml
lod: auto            # the default: models used by 100 objects or more
models:
  drum: models/drum.glb                                   # made simpler in the browser
  rack: { url: models/rack.glb, far: models/rack-low.glb } # a simpler model of your own
  pump: { url: models/pump.glb, far: { ratio: 0.3, distance: 40 } }
  sign: { url: models/sign.glb, far: false }              # never
```

- `lod`: `auto`, `true` (every model), `false` or `none`, or `{ ratio, distance }` for every model. A model's own `far` wins.
- Made in the browser, a model keeps `ratio` of its triangles (default 0.15) with meshoptimizer's simplifier, loaded from jsDelivr only when it's needed; parts too small to see from afar (under 3% of the model's size) are left out. A part with several materials is kept as it is.
- `distance`: metres from the camera; by default twelve times the model's size, and at least 15 m.
- A far model of your own is put right as its model is (`units`, `up`, `scale`…), and should stand where it does.
- Only objects drawn together have it; one in a look of its own (glowing by `effect`, see-through, animated) is drawn in full. The twin fires `lod` when a model's far version is ready.

### NVIDIA SimReady and other USD assets

[`tools/simready/`](https://github.com/kaushik-xs/iRender/blob/main/tools/simready) downloads [SimReady](https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/simready-assets) assets and converts them to GLB: Y up, in metres, standing at their base, with their materials as glTF's and their textures as WebP, simplified and compressed with meshopt. The examples' models were made this way.

## Machine and sensor data

An object's data is any of its fields. `readouts` say which to show, how, and where their limits are:

```yaml
readouts:
  - { field: temp, label: Motor, unit: °C, warn: 70, alarm: 85, history: 40, when: { kind: conveyor } }
  - { field: level, label: Level, unit: "%", decimals: 0, warn: 25, alarm: 10, below: true }
  - { field: humidity, label: Humidity, unit: "%", tag: false }
```

- An object's first two readouts are on its tag over it (`tag` says otherwise), and all of them are in its popup.
- Past `warn` an object turns warning; past `alarm` it's in alarm. `below: true` is for values that mustn't fall, like a tank's level or a battery.
- `history: n` keeps an object's last n values of a readout (a point each time it changes, up to 500) and draws them as a sparkline beside it in the popup. They're kept in the page, from when it opened; an object that leaves the world forgets them.
- `when` (a `filter`, as the data table's) or `models` limit a readout to some objects, so each kind of machine, or each room, can have its own limits.
- `colorBy: { field, min, max, colors }` colours objects along a scale by a value, e.g. temperatures from blue to red. `sensor` shapes take the colour themselves; models glow with it.

### Live values

The values can come from state (a `ui-live-data`, the host, a form), or from a feed of the twin's own:

```yaml
live: { url: /api/plant, every: 5000 }   # polled
live: { stream: /api/plant/stream }      # server-sent events
bindLive: values                         # the latest values in state, by id
```

Each answer is either a list of rows with an `id`, or `{ "<id>": { "field": value } }`. Its fields are merged into the objects with that id, over what the document says. The objects stay where the document puts them unless the feed sends a `position`, a `progress` along a path, or a `speed`: a vehicle stopped by the feed (`speed: 0`) stops where it is. A feed that can't be reached marks the twin `data-stale` (its values are dimmed) and fires `failed` once.

## Status, alarms and effects

- `toneBy: { field: status, tones: { running: success, fault: danger } }`, or `tone` on a row, draws a ring of that tone around the object's footprint. A warning or alarm from its values comes before its status's tone.
- `alarmBy: { field: status, values: [fault] }`, `alarm: true` on a row, or a readout past `alarm` puts an object in alarm. It glows red, gets a `!` tag that stays above the others (alarms side by side on screen share one, counted: `+2`), `bindAlarms` gets its id, it's announced to screen readers, and the twin fires `alarm`.
- `effectBy`, or `effect` on a row: `pulse`, `glow`, `blink`, `spin` (with `spin` in degrees a second, e.g. a fan) or `bob`. All of them hold still where the viewer asked for less motion.

## Paths and movement

An object with `path` drives along it at `speed` metres a second (default 1), turned to face its way unless `face: false`, and around again if the path is `closed` or `loop` isn't false. With `progress` (0 to 1) and no `speed`, it stands that far along: a feed can say where something is. `attach: <id>` carries an object with another, e.g. a pallet on a forklift.

An object whose `position` or `rotation` changes in the data moves there over `transition` milliseconds (default 600). `follow: <id>` keeps the camera at its distance from a moving object.

## State

| prop | holds |
|---|---|
| `bind` | the selected object's id; setting it selects that object and flies to it |
| `bindObject` | the selected object itself, with its latest values |
| `bindZone` | the id of the zone last clicked |
| `bindView` | the current view's id; setting it moves the camera there |
| `bindAlarms` | the ids of the objects in alarm |
| `bindLive` | the latest values from `live` |
| `bindCamera` | `{ position, target }` once the camera has moved: copy it into `views` |
| `bindObjects` | the objects' list, written back when they're moved, added or removed |
| `bindMeasure` | the last measurement, `{ from, to, distance, across, up }` in metres |

`filter` shows only the objects that pass, e.g. a `ui-filters` panel's `bind`, or an area picked in a toggle group.

## Popups and panels

The selected object opens a popup with its title, description and readouts. A `ui-twin-popup` child replaces that with any components, with the object in scope as `object`. `ui-twin-panel` children float above the view at a `position` (`top-left`, `bottom-right`, …), e.g. a legend or filters.

```yaml
- type: ui-twin
  props: { objects: "{{ pallets }}", bind: picked }
  children:
    - type: ui-twin-popup
      children:
        - { type: text, props: { value: "{{ object.title }}" } }
        - { type: ui-progress, props: { value: "{{ object.done * 100 / object.lines }}" } }
    - type: ui-twin-panel
      props: { position: bottom-left }
      children: [ { type: ui-badge, props: { text: "{{ alarms.length }} in alarm" } } ]
```

## Editing a layout

With `editable: true` and `bindObjects`, objects can be dragged on the ground (snapping to `snap` metres). The selected one moves with Alt and the arrow keys, turns 90° with Alt+R (Alt+Shift+R back), and Delete removes it; its popup has Rotate and Remove too. `palette` offers things to add: clicked, one goes in the middle of the view; dragged into it, where it's dropped. Each change is written back to its row in the form the row had (`[x, z]`, `[x, y, z]`, `{ x, z }` or `x` and `z` fields), and the twin fires `move`, `add` or `remove`. Objects on a path or attached to another aren't moved by hand.

### Several at once

With `multiple: true`, ⌘, Ctrl or Shift and a click adds an object to the ones picked or takes it away (on the view, its tag or the list), Shift and a drag from the floor draws a box and picks what's in it, and ⌘A (with the view focused) picks them all. Each picked one has its ring; the last one picked is the selected one (`bind`, its popup when it's alone), and `bindSelected` has all their ids (set it to pick them). Editable, they move together: dragging one drags the others with it, Alt and the arrows move them all, Alt+R turns each about itself, and Delete removes them all, written back in one change. The twin fires `selectionchange` with `{ ids, objects }`, and `selectMany(ids)` and `selection` are on the element's `__twin`.

## Measuring

With `measure: true` the controls have a ruler (M with the view focused does the same). Turned on, two clicks on objects, walls or the floor draw a line between them with its length; when it slopes, how far across and how far up as well. Picked from a tag or the objects' list (so from the keyboard too), an object counts from its middle on the floor. A third click starts again, and Escape (or the ruler) stops. The line is drawn over everything, so one through a wall still shows. `bindMeasure` holds the last one, the twin fires `measure` with it, and `measure(a, b)` on the element's `__twin` takes two ids or points (`[x, z]` or `[x, y, z]`) and draws it; `measure(null)` clears it.

## Events

| event | detail |
|---|---|
| `ready` | `{ objects }`, once the models have loaded |
| `select` | `{ id, object }` |
| `selectionchange` | `{ ids, objects }`, with `multiple` |
| `zoneselect` | `{ id, zone }` |
| `alarm` | `{ id, object }`, for each new alarm |
| `data` | `{ count }`, for each answer from `live` |
| `measure` | `{ from, to, distance, across, up }` |
| `move`, `add`, `remove` | `{ id, position, rotation }` or `{ id, object }` |
| `failed` | `{ error }`, with `model` or `live` when that's what failed |

## Gestures and keys

Drag to turn the view, right-drag (or two fingers) to move it, and scroll or pinch to zoom. `gestures: none` keeps the camera where the document puts it. The view takes the focus: the arrow keys turn it, Shift and the arrows move it, + and − zoom, and Home fits the world. The objects are also a list for the keyboard and screen readers, after the view: it shows while it has the focus, and picking one selects it and flies to it. Escape closes the popup, then the selection. With `measure`, M turns the ruler on and off. With `multiple`, Shift-drag from the floor draws a box (see [Several at once](#several-at-once)); otherwise it moves the view as right-drag does.

## Smoothness

A twin draws a frame only when something changed: the camera, an object, the data. Three things keep those frames short:

- **Shadows are drawn again only when something that casts one changes.** The sun's shadows don't depend on the camera, so turning or zooming the view costs no shadow pass. Objects that move on their own (on a path, spinning) redraw them at most every 50 ms; a change from the data, a drag or a model loading redraws them at once.
- **Objects of the same model are drawn together** (instancing): a few draw calls per model however many objects use it. Those in alarm are instances too, of their own, glowing together; those coloured by value (`colorBy`) are instances that each glow in their own colour; so are the rings on the ground under warnings (one draw call for each size of ring). Shapes are drawn together too, one batch for each kind and size, each in its own colour (a sensor glowing in its value's). An object that needs a look of its own (glowing or blinking by `effect`, see-through, animated, a shape in alarm) is drawn as a copy of its own for as long as it does, so nothing looks different. A batch that glows by instance is shown once its shaders are compiled, in the background.
- **Only what's in view is drawn:** as the camera moves, the instances outside it are left out, so a big world seen up close draws the objects near the camera.
- **Far away, models are simpler** (`lod`, see [Simpler far away](#simpler-far-away)).
- **Tags are placed in one pass:** measured first, then moved, with only the styles that changed written, and moved only when the view or something in it has (not while alarms just glow). Tags that would overlap are found by where they are on screen, not against every other tag.
- **While the camera moves, the view is drawn at a lower resolution** (`motionScale`, default 0.65 of the pixels each way, so about 40% of them), and sharp again 400 ms after it stops. Only the camera's moving counts: objects moving on their own keep a still view sharp. `motionScale: 1` turns it off.
- **A model's GPU work is done before it's shown:** its shaders compile in the background (in parallel where the browser can) and its textures go up a few at a time, instead of all in the first frame that draws it.

On a laptop (Apple M4 Pro, Chrome), turning the camera around block twin-01 (38 objects, about 1.2 million triangles) holds 60 frames a second with no frame over 20 ms; the page is blocked for about 130 ms while it loads, most of it three.js itself. `quality: low` turns shadows and smoothing off for slower devices.

Bigger worlds (2026-11-26, the same laptop, a grid of six models of 5,000 to 60,000 triangles each with a readout and a tag on every object, a quarter of them warning or in alarm):

| objects | ready | still | turning | close up | every value changing 4× a second |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 300 | 0.7 s | 60 fps | 60 fps | 60 fps | 60 fps |
| 1,000 | 1.0 s | 61 | 58–59 | 56–60 | 59 |
| 3,000 | 1.1 s | 47–51 | 43 | 41–56 | 34–36 |

With `lod` (the default), 1,000 of these objects are 6 to 8 million triangles instead of 39 million. Without it, 1,000 objects run at 45–53 fps still and 43 turning, and 3,000 at 19 and 14–16. At 3,000, the tags cost more than the models: `labels: none` (alarms only) turns at 48. Example: [twin/big-world](https://github.com/kaushik-xs/iRender/blob/main/examples/twin/big-world.yaml).

## three.js

three.js isn't inlined. A page loads it as ES modules, once, from jsDelivr, when a twin comes near the view, along with the loaders its models need. [`TwinKit`](https://github.com/kaushik-xs/iRender/blob/main/crates/irender-twin-kit/src/lib.rs) points it elsewhere, e.g. your own copy:

```rust
irender_twin_kit::register_with(&mut engine.registry, irender_twin_kit::TwinKit {
    three: "/static/three/three.module.js".into(),
    addons: "/static/three/jsm/{name}".into(),   // must import three.js from the same address
    draco: "/static/three/draco/".into(),
    basis: "/static/three/basis/".into(),
    simplifier: "/static/meshopt_simplifier.js".into(), // meshoptimizer's, for `lod`
});
```

The kit is written and tested against three.js 0.183.2 ([`THREE_VERSION`](https://github.com/kaushik-xs/iRender/blob/main/crates/irender-twin-kit/src/lib.rs)) and meshoptimizer 1.3.0 ([`MESHOPT_VERSION`](https://github.com/kaushik-xs/iRender/blob/main/crates/irender-twin-kit/src/lib.rs)), whose simplifier is loaded only when a model is made simpler far away.

## Safety

Model, world and feed URLs are checked against the document's policy on the server when they're known there, and in the browser when they come from state. Documents the policy doesn't trust can't point a model or an object's `href` at a script.

## When it can't draw

Without WebGL (or three.js), the twin says so and lists its objects, with their readouts and alarms, so the values are still there.

## Not built yet

See [PENDING.md](https://github.com/kaushik-xs/iRender/blob/main/PENDING.md#twin-kit-next-phases).


---


# irender-icon-kit

SVG icons for [iRender](https://github.com/kaushik-xs/iRender/blob/main/README.md) documents: `ui-icon`, with packs of original icons for everyday interfaces and for industries, each in an outline and a filled style, and your own packs from SVG files.

```rust
let mut engine = irender_html::Engine::new();
irender_icon_kit::register(&mut engine.registry);   // every built-in pack
```

From the CLI, add `--icon-kit` to `validate`, `render` or `components`, and list what ships with `icons`:

```sh
cargo run -p irender-cli -- render page.yaml --ui-kit --icon-kit -o page.html
cargo run -p irender-cli -- icons              # packs and icon names
cargo run -p irender-cli -- icons logistics    # one pack
cargo run -p irender-cli -- icons --json       # for tooling, or as page data
```

```yaml
- { type: ui-icon, props: { name: logistics:truck } }
- { type: ui-icon, props: { name: check, size: 16, label: Delivered }, style: { color: $color.primary } }
- { type: ui-icon, props: { name: retail:shopping-cart, variant: filled } }
```

## `ui-icon`

| prop | |
|---|---|
| `name` | `pack:icon`, e.g. `logistics:truck`, or a bare `icon`, found in the first pack that has it. Required. |
| `variant` | `outline` (default) or `filled`. |
| `size` | Number (px) or CSS length. Default `1em`, the size of the text around it. May use state. |
| `label` | Accessible name (`role="img"`, `aria-label`). Without it the icon is decorative and `aria-hidden`. |

- Strokes are always 2 grid units, the width the icons are drawn and spaced for, so there's no prop to change it.
- The icon is an inline `<svg>` drawn in `currentColor`, so `color` (or the surrounding text) sets it. `attrs`, `class` and `style` apply to the `<svg>` as usual.
- Only the icons a page uses are sent: there's no sprite or font to load.
- `name` and `variant` are resolved on the server. They can come from server data (`"{{ order.icon }}"`), but not from `state`. To switch icons in the browser (say, outline to filled when an item is selected), use `if` / `else` with one `ui-icon` in each branch.
- An unknown name is a render error that suggests close names (`unknown icon `trcuk`; did you mean `logistics:truck`?`).

## Built-in packs

| pack | contents |
|---|---|
| `core` | Everyday interface actions and objects: add, edit, delete, search, filter, settings, share, lock, users, calendar, time. |
| `arrows` | Arrows, chevrons, carets, corners, rotation, swap and move. |
| `status` | States of a task or record: done, failed, pending, blocked, draft, archived, scheduled, overdue, sync, online. |
| `logistics` | Transport, shipping and delivery: vehicles, parcels, containers, docks, routes and proof of delivery. |
| `warehouse` | Warehouse operations and inventory: racks, bins, picking, packing, stock levels, counts, lots and serials. |
| `retail` | Stores and e-commerce: carts, checkout, POS, products, promotions, orders, reviews and loyalty. |
| `manufacturing` | Factories and production: machines, tools, components, process equipment, quality, maintenance and safety. |
| `accounting` | Accounting operations: payables and receivables, accounts and entries, notes, accruals and depreciation, assets and cost centres, close and tax. |
| `agriculture` | Farming: machinery, crops, fields, irrigation, soil, livestock, beekeeping and harvest. |
| `automotive` | Road vehicles: cars, bikes and buses, mobility services, dealerships, keys and plates, parts, servicing, dashboard warnings and roadside help. |
| `aviation` | Airports and flight: aircraft, terminals, gates, runways, baggage, security and flight status. |
| `banking` | Banks and payments: branches and ATMs, cards and wallets, cash, accounts, transfers, lending, currencies and compliance. |
| `construction` | Building sites and real estate: heavy equipment, trades and tools, plans, buildings, site paperwork and safety. |
| `education` | Schools and e-learning: buildings, books and supplies, people, courses, assessment, timetables and subjects. |
| `energy` | Power and utilities: generation, renewables, the grid, meters, storage, EV charging and efficiency. |
| `finance` | Markets and accounting: charts, investing, assets and risk, ledgers and statements, budgets, tax, audit and forecasts. |
| `healthcare` | Hospitals and clinical care: facilities, instruments, medicines, vital signs, diagnostics, staff and records. |
| `hospitality` | Hotels, restaurants and leisure: rooms and keys, guest services, food and drink, dining and amenities. |
| `hr` | Human resources: hiring, people and org, payroll, time and leave, performance and learning, benefits and wellbeing. |
| `insurance` | Policies and claims: cover, premiums, claims and their status, underwriting, people and lines of insurance. |
| `it` | IT and software: servers, cloud, networking gear, development and DevOps, data, monitoring and security. |
| `legal` | Law and compliance: courts and people, contracts and signatures, evidence, rulings, privacy and intellectual property. |
| `marketing` | Marketing: campaigns, audiences and targeting, funnels and conversion, SEO, social and email, ads, brand and analytics. |
| `maritime` | Shipping and the sea: vessels, ports and berths, cargo handling, navigation, safety equipment, tides and voyages. |
| `media` | Media production and distribution: film, TV, radio and podcasts, audio and video, photography, print and news, streaming. |
| `mining` | Mines and quarries: shafts, tunnels, open pits, heavy equipment, ore, processing, geology and safety. |
| `oil-gas` | Oil and gas, upstream to downstream: rigs, wells, pipelines, refining, storage, transport, fuel and leaks. |
| `public-sector` | Government and civic services: buildings, elections, IDs and permits, emergency services, transport, streets and utilities. |
| `robotics` | Robots and automation: arms, grippers, mobile and legged robots, drones, actuators, sensors and safety. |
| `simulation` | Simulation and digital twins: models, scenarios, runs, parameters, randomness, meshes, physics and results. |
| `space` | Spaceflight and astronomy: rockets, satellites, stations, astronauts, planets, stars and ground stations. |
| `social` | Social networks, without logos: likes and votes, comments and replies, reposts and messages, following, profiles, feeds and stories, polls and moderation. |
| `sports` | Sports and fitness: trophies and venues, balls and equipment, athletes in motion, workouts and tracking, teams and officiating. |
| `telecom` | Telecom networks: towers and antennas, signal and coverage, SIMs and phones, calls and messages, fibre and plans. |

| `brands` | Logo marks of social networks and sign-in providers (see below). |

Bare names are looked up in `core`, `arrows` and `status` first, then the industry packs alphabetically, and `brands` last. Write `pack:icon` whenever two packs might have the same name. The [icon gallery](https://github.com/kaushik-xs/iRender/blob/main/examples/icons/gallery.yaml) shows every icon.

More industry packs are planned; see [PENDING.md](https://github.com/kaushik-xs/iRender/blob/main/PENDING.md).

### Logo marks

`brands` holds 56 logos: social networks (`facebook`, `instagram`, `x`, `threads`, `youtube`, `tiktok`, `reddit`, `discord`, `mastodon`, `bluesky`, …), messengers (`whatsapp`, `telegram`, `signal`, `wechat`, `line`, …), developer and creator sites (`github`, `gitlab`, `stack-overflow`, `dribbble`, `behance`, `medium`, `substack`, …) and sign-in providers (`google`, `apple`, `meta`, `slack`). `irender icons brands` lists them all.

```yaml
- { type: ui-button, props: { label: Login with Google, icon: brands:google, variant: outline } }
- { type: ui-icon, props: { name: brands:github, label: GitHub, size: 20 } }
```

- They aren't drawn for the kit. The paths come from [Simple Icons](https://simpleicons.org) 15.0.0 (CC0), unchanged, and are solid single-colour marks in `currentColor`. A `viewBox` of `-2 -2 28 28` gives them the same 2 px padding as the kit's icons.
- `variant: filled` draws the same mark.
- The logos are trademarks of their owners. Use them to point to those services (a profile link, "Sign in with …") and follow each brand's guidelines.
- Some brands aren't available: LinkedIn and Microsoft asked Simple Icons to remove their logos. Add them as your own pack (below) from the owners' brand kits.

### How the icons are drawn

Every built-in icon was drawn for this kit, not taken from another set, to one standard: a 24 px grid with 2 px padding, 2 px round strokes, shared keylines, a half-pixel grid, modifiers in the bottom-right corner and at most about 8 shapes. [GUIDELINES.md](https://github.com/kaushik-xs/iRender/blob/main/crates/irender-icon-kit/GUIDELINES.md) is the full standard.

The filled style is drawn on the outline's own centrelines, filled *and* stroked, so its silhouette matches the outline's outer edge and the two swap without the icon shifting; inner details become cut-outs. Icons with nothing to fill (arrows, check, close, …) use their outline drawing for both styles; each pack lists them in `filled/_same.txt`.

To add or change an icon:

```sh
crates/irender-icon-kit/tools/icons.py lint                       # the measurable rules
crates/irender-icon-kit/tools/icons.py sheet logistics -o s.html  # a contact sheet at 96, 24 and 16 px, light and dark
crates/irender-icon-kit/tools/icons.py sheet logistics --filled -o s.html   # the filled style beside the outline
```

## Your own packs

```rust
use irender_icon_kit::{IconKit, Pack};

let brand = Pack::from_dir("brand", "assets/icons")?;      // every *.svg; `Box Truck.svg` → `box-truck`; filled ones from assets/icons/filled/
let kit = IconKit::new().with(brand);                       // built-ins first, then yours
irender_icon_kit::register_with(&mut engine.registry, kit);

// Or your names first, with only the built-in packs you want:
let kit = IconKit::empty().with(brand).with_builtin("core")?.with_builtin("logistics")?;

// Or from strings:
let mut pack = Pack::new("brand", "Brand")?;
pack.add_svg("logo", include_str!("logo.svg"))?;
pack.add_svg_filled("logo", include_str!("logo-filled.svg"))?;   // optional: `variant: filled`
pack.same_when_filled("divider")?;                               // or: the outline serves both
```

CLI: `--icons assets/icons` (a pack named after the directory) or `--icons brand=assets/icons`, repeatable; it implies `--icon-kit`.

Any SVG works, at any `viewBox`. On load it's reduced to its shapes (`path`, `circle`, `ellipse`, `rect`, `line`, `polyline`, `polygon`, `g`), their geometry and drawing attributes, and the root's `viewBox` and drawing defaults (`fill`, `stroke`, `stroke-width`, …). Scripts, styles, links, text, `<use>`, images, gradients, event attributes and `url(…)` references are dropped, so a pack file can't put anything else into a page. For icons that follow the text colour, draw them with `currentColor` (or no colour at all for fills).
